# Bioresorbable Vascular Scaffolds in Percutaneous Coronary Intervention: A Narrative Review

Percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) has undergone significant evolutionary milestones over the last four decades. The field progressed from plain old balloon angioplasty (POBA) to bare-metal stents (BMS), and ultimately to current-generation drug-eluting metallic stents (DES). While modern metallic DES have achieved excellent safety and efficacy profiles, they leave behind a permanent metallic cage. This permanent foreign body imposes several long-term limitations, including chronic inflammatory responses, neoatherosclerosis, late stent thrombosis, physical restriction of natural vasomotor function, and the obstruction of future surgical bypass options [1]. 

To overcome these disadvantages, the paradigm of "vascular restoration therapy" emerged, introducing the concept of bioresorbable vascular scaffolds (BVS) [2,3]. Designed to provide temporary mechanical support and antiproliferative drug delivery during the critical healing phase, these transient devices undergo progressive resorption, leaving behind a native vessel restored to its physiological state [2,3].

### First-Generation Polymeric Scaffolds and Early Feasibility
The earliest clinical evaluations of a bioresorbable scaffold used the Absorb everolimus-eluting PLLA-based BVS (Abbott Vascular). Early feasibility trials, such as the ABSORB Cohort A, showed promising initial safety and efficacy, demonstrating excellent device patency and complete resorption over several years [4,5]. The subsequent ABSORB Cohort B trial utilized advanced intravascular imaging to confirm the restoration of vasomotion and late luminal enlargement [6], with ultra-long-term follow-up demonstrating safety out to 10 years [7]. Based on these pioneering data, the first-generation polymeric BVS received clinical approval and was rapidly adopted into broader clinical practice [8,9].

### Pivotal Trials and Major Setbacks
Despite initial optimism, larger randomized clinical trials comparing the Absorb BVS against the gold-standard metallic everolimus-eluting stent (EES; XIENCE) revealed substantial safety concerns, leading to cautious consensus reports from major scientific societies [10]. The landmark, large-scale ABSORB III trial achieved its primary non-inferiority endpoint of target lesion failure (TLF) at 1 year, but raised concern due to a numerical signal of increased scaffold thrombosis (ScT) and target vessel myocardial infarction [11]. Long-term data confirmed these fears, showing significantly higher rates of TLF and device thrombosis with BVS at 3 years [12] and 5 years [13].

This safety signal was further reinforced by several independent studies. The Dutch AIDA trial was halted early by its data safety monitoring board due to a significantly higher incidence of scaffold thrombosis in BVS-treated patients compared to those receiving EES [14]. Furthermore, the ABSORB IV trial [15], the ABSORB Japan trial [16], and real-world registries such as GHOST-EU [17] and INVEST ASSURE [18] consistently demonstrated an elevated risk of both early and late scaffold thrombosis. Extensive systematic reviews and meta-analyses pooled these outcomes, confirming a two- to three-fold higher risk of scaffold thrombosis with first-generation BVS compared to EES, particularly in small vessel interventions [19-22].

### Pathophysiological Underpinnings and Implantation Techniques
Comprehensive intravascular imaging evaluations, such as optical coherence tomography (OCT) studies, have elucidated the main drivers of first-generation BVS failure. The primary limitation stemmed from the physical properties of the polymeric material: to match the radial strength of metallic stents, polymeric struts had to be considerably thicker (~150 µm compared to ~60–80 µm for metallic DES). These bulky struts compromised local hemodynamic flow, promoted platelet aggregation, and increased under-expansion, malapposition, and late scaffold dismantling during resorption [23].

These failures emphasized that BVS implantation is highly technique-dependent. Expert consensus panels proposed the "PSP" protocol: meticulous pre-dilation (P), accurate vessel sizing (S), and high-pressure post-dilation (P) using non-compliant balloons [24,25]. Clinical registries demonstrated that when the PSP protocol was strictly followed, scaffold under-expansion and malapposition decreased, translating to clinical outcome improvements and narrower safety gaps between BVS and metallic DES [24,25].

### Next-Generation Devices and Future Horizons
Acknowledging the mechanical limits of thick-strut polymeric scaffolds, the field transitioned toward thinner-strut designs and alternative materials [3]. Magnesium-based scaffolds, such as the Magmaris (Biotronik), offered a metallic structure with superior radial strength, allowing thinner struts and faster resorption (approximately 12 months). The BIOSOLVE-II trial demonstrated the safety and efficacy of Magmaris, reporting favorable late lumen loss and no definite scaffold thrombosis [26,27]. Subsequent data from BIOSOLVE-III confirmed these results, validating magnesium-based BVS as a safe and effective therapeutic option [28].

Simultaneously, newer thin-strut polymeric scaffolds have emerged. The Fantom scaffold (Reva Medical), composed of a desaminotyrosine polycarbonate polymer, provides radiopacity and thinner struts [29]. Similarly, the Firesorb scaffold (MicroPort), a thin-strut PLLA-based BVS, has shown promising safety and angiographic results in early clinical evaluations [30].

### Conclusion
The journey of bioresorbable vascular scaffolds represents a dramatic and instructive chapter in interventional cardiology. While first-generation thick-strut polymeric devices faced clinical setbacks due to scaffold thrombosis, they drove vital advancements in implantation protocols and intravascular imaging. With the advent of modern thin-strut polymeric and magnesium-based platforms, the promise of complete vascular restoration remains a viable and highly promising goal in coronary interventions.
